speaker: CLINTON
text: The length of the printed transcript is approximately 14 pages long.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right, moving on now to divisions in our country, the first question goes to Governor Clinton for 2 minutes, and Ann will ask it.

speaker: COMPTON
text: Governor Clinton, can you tell us what your definition of the word “family” is?

speaker: CLINTON
text: A family involves at least one parent, whether natural or adoptive or foster, and children.

speaker: CLINTON
text: A good family is a place where love and discipline and good values are transmuted from the elders to the children, a place where people turn for refuge, and where they know they’re the most important people in the world.

speaker: CLINTON
text: America has a lot of families that are in trouble today.

speaker: CLINTON
text: There’s been a lot of talk about family values in this campaign.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I know a lot about that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I was born to a widowed mother who gave me family values, and grandparents.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve seen the family values of my people in Arkansas.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve seen the family values of all these people in America who are out there killing themselves working harder for less in a country that’s had the worst economic years in 50 years and the first decline in industrial production ever.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I think the president owes it to family values to show that he values America’s families, whether they’re people on welfare you’re trying to move from welfare to work, the working poor whom I think deserve a tax break to lift them above poverty if they’ve got a child in the house and working 40 hours a week, working families who deserve a fair tax system and the opportunity for constant retraining; they deserve a strong economy.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I think they deserve a family and medical leave act.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Seventy-two other nations have been able to do it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Bush vetoed it twice because he says we can’t do something seventy-two other countries do, even though there was a small business exemption.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So with all the talk about family values, I know about family values — I wouldn’t be here without them.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The best expression of my family values is that tonight’s my 17th wedding anniversary, and I’d like to close my question by just wishing my wife a happy anniversary, and thank you, my daughter, for being here.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President Bush, one minute.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, I would say that one meeting that made a profound impression on me was when the mayors of the big cities, including the mayor of Los Angeles, a Democrat, came to see me, and they unanimously said the decline in urban America stems from the decline in the American family.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I do think we need to strengthen family.

speaker: BUSH
text: When Barbara holds an AIDS baby, she’s showing a certain compassion for family; when she reads to children, the same thing.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe that discipline and respect for the law — all of these things should be taught to children, not in our schools, but families have to do that.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m appalled at the highest outrageous numbers of divorces — it happens in families, it’s happened in ours.

speaker: BUSH
text: But it’s gotten too much.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I just think that we ought to do everything we can to respect the American family.

speaker: BUSH
text: It can be a single-parent family.

speaker: BUSH
text: Those mothers need help.

speaker: BUSH
text: And one way to do it is to get these deadbeat fathers to pay their obligations to these mothers — that will help strengthen the American family.

speaker: BUSH
text: And there’s a whole bunch of other things that I can’t click off in this short period of time.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right, Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Perot, you have one minute.

speaker: PEROT
text: If I had to solve all the problems that face this country and I could be granted one wish as we started down the trail to rebuild the job base, the schools and so on and so forth, I would say a strong family unit in every home, where every child is loved, nurtured, and encouraged.

speaker: PEROT
text: A little child before they’re 18 months learns to think well of himself or herself or poorly.

speaker: PEROT
text: They develop a positive or negative self- image.

speaker: PEROT
text: At a very early age they learn how to learn.

speaker: PEROT
text: If we have children who are not surrounded with love and affection — you see, I look at my grandchildren and wonder if they’ll ever learn to walk because they’re always in someone’s arms.

speaker: PEROT
text: And I think, my gosh, wouldn’t it be wonderful if every child had that love and support.

speaker: PEROT
text: But they don’t.

speaker: PEROT
text: We will not be a great country unless we have a strong family unit in every home.

speaker: PEROT
text: And I think you can use the White House as a bully pulpit to stress the importance of these little children, particularly in their young and formative years, to mold these little precious pieces of clay so that they, too, can live rich full lives when they’re grown.

speaker: LEHRER
text: New question, two-minute answer, goes to President Bush.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Sandy will ask it.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: Mr.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: President, there’s been a lot of talk about Harry Truman in this campaign, so much so that I think tomorrow I’ll wake up and see him named as the next commissioner of baseball.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: The thing that Mr.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: Truman didn’t have to deal with is drugs.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: Americans are increasingly alarmed about drug-related crimes in cities and suburbs.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: And your administration is not the first to have grappled with this.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: And are you at all of a mind that maybe it ought to go to another level, if not to what’s advocated by William F.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: Buckley, Jr.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: and Milton Friedman, legalization, somewhere between there and where we are now?

speaker: BUSH
text: No, I don’t think that’s the right answer.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t believe legalizing narcotics is the answer.

speaker: BUSH
text: I just don’t believe that’s the answer.

speaker: BUSH
text: I do believe that there’s some fairly good news out there.

speaker: BUSH
text: The use of cocaine, for example, by teenagers is dramatically down.

speaker: BUSH
text: But we’ve got to keep fighting on this war against drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re doing a little better in interdiction.

speaker: BUSH
text: Many of the countries below that used to say, well, this is the US’ problem — if you’d get the demand down, then we wouldn’t have the problem — are working cooperatively with the DEA and the military.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re using the military more now in terms of interdiction.

speaker: BUSH
text: Our funding for recovery is up, recovering the addicts.

speaker: BUSH
text: Where we’re not making the progress, Sander, is in — we’re making it in teenagers, and thank God, because I thought what Ross said was most appropriate about these families and these children.

speaker: BUSH
text: But where we’re not making it is with the confirmed addicts.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I’ll tell you one place that’s working well, and that is the private sector — Jim Burke and this task force that he has, you may know about it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ll tell the American people, but this man said I’ll get you a million dollars a day in pro bono advertising, something that’s very hard for the government to do.

speaker: BUSH
text: And he went out and he did it.

speaker: BUSH
text: And people are beginning to educate through this program, teaching these kids you shouldn’t use drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: So we’re still in the fight.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I must tell you, I think legalization of narcotics, or something of that nature, in the face of the medical evidence, would be totally counterproductive.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I oppose it, and I’m going to stand up and continue to oppose it.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Perot, one minute.

speaker: PEROT
text: Anytime you think you want to legalize drugs, go to a neonatal unit — if you can get in.

speaker: PEROT
text: They’re between 100 and 200% capacity up and down the East Coast.

speaker: PEROT
text: And the reason is crack babies being born, babies in the hospital 42 days.

speaker: PEROT
text: Typical cost to you and me is $125,000.

speaker: PEROT
text: Again and again and again, the mother disappears in 3 days, and the child becomes a ward of the state because he’s permanently and genetically damaged.

speaker: PEROT
text: Just look at those little children, and if anybody can even think about legalizing drugs, they’ve lost me.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, let’s look at priorities.

speaker: PEROT
text: You know, we went on the Libyan raid — do you remember that one?

speaker: PEROT
text: — because we were worried to death that Gaddafi might be building up chemical weapons.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’ve got chemical warfare being conducted against our children on the streets in this country all day every day, and we don’t have the will to stamp it out.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, again, if I get up there, if you send me, we’re going to have some blunt talks about this, and we’re really going to get down in the trenches and say, is this one you want to talk about or fix, because talk won’t do it, folks.

speaker: PEROT
text: There are guys that couldn’t get a job third shift in a Dairy Queen driving BMWs and Mercedes selling drugs.

speaker: PEROT
text: And these old boys are not going to quit easy.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Governor Clinton, one minute.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Like Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Perot, I have held crack babies in my arms.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But I know more about this, I think, than anybody else up here because I have a brother who’s a recovering drug addict.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’m very proud of him.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But I can tell you this.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If drugs were legal, I don’t think he’d be alive today.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I am adamantly opposed to legalizing drugs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: He is alive today because of the criminal justice system.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That’s a mistake.

speaker: CLINTON
text: What should we do?

speaker: CLINTON
text: First, we ought to prevent more of this on the street.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Thirty years ago, there were three policemen for every crime.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now there are three crimes for every policeman.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need a hundred thousand more police on the street.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I have a plan for that.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Secondly, we ought to have treatment on demand.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Thirdly, we ought to have boot camps for first-time nonviolent offenders so they can get discipline and treatment and education and get reconnected to the community before they’re severed and sent to prison, where they can learn how to be first class criminals.

speaker: CLINTON
text: There is a crime bill that, lamentably, was blocked from passage once again, mostly by Republicans in the US Senate, which would have addressed some of these problems.

speaker: CLINTON
text: That crime bill is going to be one of my highest priorities next January if I become president.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Next question is to you, Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Perot.

speaker: LEHRER
text: You have two minutes to answer it and John will ask it.

speaker: MASHEK
text: Mr.

speaker: MASHEK
text: Perot, racial division continues to tear apart our great cities, the last episode being this spring in Los Angeles.

speaker: MASHEK
text: Why is this still happening in America, and what would you do to end it?

speaker: PEROT
text: This is a relevant question here tonight.

speaker: PEROT
text: The first thing I’d do is, during political campaigns, I would urge everybody to stop trying to split this country into fragments and appeal to the differences between us and then wonder why the melting pot is all broken to pieces after November the 3rd.

speaker: PEROT
text: We are all in this together.

speaker: PEROT
text: We ought to love one another because united teams win and divided teams lose.

speaker: PEROT
text: And if we can’t love one another, we ought to get along with one another.

speaker: PEROT
text: And if you can’t get there, just recognize we’re all stuck with one another because nobody’s going anywhere, right?

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, that ought to get everybody back up to let’s get along together and make it work.

speaker: PEROT
text: Our diversity is a strength.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’ve turned it into a weakness.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now again, the White House is a bully pulpit.

speaker: PEROT
text: I think whoever is in the White House should just make it absolutely unconscionable and inexcusable, and if anybody’s in the middle of a speech at, you know, one of these conventions, I would expect the candidate to go out and lift him off the stage if he starts preaching hate — because we don’t have time for it.

speaker: PEROT
text: See, our differences are our strengths.

speaker: PEROT
text: We have got to pull together.

speaker: PEROT
text: In athletics, we know it.

speaker: PEROT
text: See, divided teams lose; united teams win.

speaker: PEROT
text: We have got to unite and pull together, and there’s nothing we can’t do.

speaker: PEROT
text: But if we sit around blowing all this energy out the window on racial strife and hatred, we are stuck with a sure loser because we have been a melting pot.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’re becoming more and more of a melting pot.

speaker: PEROT
text: Let’s make it a strength, not a weakness.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Governor Clinton, one minute.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I grew up in the segregated South, thankfully raised by a grandfather with almost no formal education but with a heart of gold who taught me early that all people were equal in the eyes of God.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I saw the winds of hatred divide people and keep the people of my state poorer than they would have been, spiritually and economically.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I’ve done everything I could in my public life to overcome racial divisions.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We don’t have a person to waste in this country.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We are being murdered economically because we have too many drop-outs, we have too many low birthweight babies, we have too many drug addicts as kids, we have too much violence, we are too divided by race, by income, by region.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I have devoted a major portion of this campaign to going across this country and looking for opportunities to go to white groups and African American groups and Latino groups and Asian American groups and say the same thing.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If the American people cannot be brought together, we can’t turn this country around.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If we can come together, nothing can stop us.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President, one minute.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, I think Governor Clinton is committed.

speaker: BUSH
text: I do think it’s fair to note — he can rebut it — but Arkansas is one of the few states that doesn’t have any civil rights legislation.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve tried to use the White House as a bully pulpit, speaking out against discrimination.

speaker: BUSH
text: We passed two very forward-looking civil rights bills.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s not going to be all done by legislation.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I do think that you need to make an appeal every time you can to eliminate racial divisions and discrimination, and I’ll keep on doing that and pointing to some legislative accomplishment to back it up.

speaker: BUSH
text: I have to take ten seconds here at the end — the red light isn’t on yet — to say to Ross Perot, please don’t say to the DEA agents on the street that we don’t have the will to fight drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: Please.

speaker: BUSH
text: I have watched these people — the same for our local law enforcement people.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re backing up at every way we possibly can.

speaker: BUSH
text: But maybe you meant that some in the country don’t have the will to fight it, but those that are out there on the front line, as you know — you’ve been a strong backer of law enforcement — really — I just want to clear that up –have the will to fight it, and, frankly, some of them are giving their lives.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Time, Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Let’s go now to another subject, the subject of health.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The first question for 2 minutes is to President Bush, and John will ask it.

speaker: MASHEK
text: Mr.

speaker: MASHEK
text: President, yesterday tens of thousands of people paraded past the White House to demonstrate their concern about the disease AIDS.

speaker: MASHEK
text: A celebrated member of your commission, Magic Johnson, quit saying that there was too much inaction.

speaker: MASHEK
text: Where is this widespread feeling coming from that your administration is not doing enough about AIDS?

speaker: BUSH
text: Coming from the political process.

speaker: BUSH
text: We have increased funding for AIDS.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve doubled it on research and on every other aspect of it.

speaker: BUSH
text: My request for this year was $4.

speaker: BUSH
text: 9 billion for AIDS — ten times as much per AIDS victim as per cancer victim.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think that we’re showing the proper compassion and concern.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I can’t tell you where it’s coming from, but I am very much concerned about AIDS and I believe that we’ve got the best researchers in the world out there at NIH working the problem.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re funding them Ã¢â‚¬â€œ I wish there was more money — but we’re funding them far more than any time in the past, and we’re going to keep on doing that.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t know.

speaker: BUSH
text: I was a little disappointed in Magic because he came to me and I said, “Now if you see something we’re not doing, get ahold of me.

speaker: BUSH
text: Call me, let me know.

speaker: BUSH
text: ” He went to one meeting, and then we heard that he was stepping down.

speaker: BUSH
text: So he’s replaced by Mary Fisher who electrified the Republican Convention by talking about the compassion and the concern that we feel.

speaker: BUSH
text: It was a beautiful moment and I think she’ll do a first-class job on that commission.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I think the appeal is yes, we care.

speaker: BUSH
text: And the other thing is part of AIDS — it’s one of the few diseases where behavior matters.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I once called on somebody, “Well, change your behavior.

speaker: BUSH
text: Is the behavior you’re using prone to cause AIDS?

speaker: BUSH
text: Change the behavior.

speaker: BUSH
text: ” Next thing I know, one of these ACT UP groups is out saying, “Bush ought to change his behavior.

speaker: BUSH
text: ” You can’t talk about it rationally.

speaker: BUSH
text: The extremes are hurting the AIDS cause.

speaker: BUSH
text: To go into a Catholic mass in a beautiful cathedral in New York under the cause of helping in AIDS and start throwing condoms around in the mass, I’m sorry, I think it sets back the cause.

speaker: BUSH
text: We cannot move to the extreme.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve got to care.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve got to continue everything we can at the federal and the local level.

speaker: BUSH
text: Barbara I think is doing a superb job in destroying the myth about AIDS.

speaker: BUSH
text: And all of us are in this fight together, all of us care.

speaker: BUSH
text: Do not go to the extreme.

speaker: LEHRER
text: One minute, Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Perot.

speaker: PEROT
text: First, I think Mary Fisher was a great choice.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’re lucky to have her heading the commission.

speaker: PEROT
text: Secondly, I think one thing that if I were sent to do the job, I would sit down with FDA, look at exactly where we are.

speaker: PEROT
text: Then I would really focus on let’s get these things out.

speaker: PEROT
text: If you’re going to die, you don’t have to go through this ten-year cycle that FDA goes through on new drugs.

speaker: PEROT
text: Believe me, people with AIDS are more than willing to take that risk.

speaker: PEROT
text: And we could be moving out to the human population a whole lot faster than we are on some of these new drugs.

speaker: PEROT
text: So I would think we can expedite the problem there.

speaker: PEROT
text: Let me go back a minute to racial divisiveness.

speaker: PEROT
text: The all- time low in our country was the Judge Thomas-Anita Hill hearings, and those senators ought to be hanging their heads in shame for what they did there.

speaker: PEROT
text: 2nd thing, there are not many times in your life when you get to talk to a whole country.

speaker: PEROT
text: But let me just say to all of America: if you hate people, I don’t want your vote.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s how strongly I feel about it.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Governor Clinton, one minute.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Over 150,000 Americans have died of AIDS.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Well over a million and a quarter Americans are HIV-positive.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need to put one person in charge of the battle against AIDS to cut across all the agencies that deal with it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need to accelerate the drug approval process.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We need to fully fund the act named for that wonderful boy Ryan White to make sure we’re doing everything we can on research and treatment.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And the president should lead a national effort to change behavior, to keep our children alive in the schools, responsible behavior to keep people alive.

speaker: CLINTON
text: This is a matter of life and death.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I have worked in my state to reduce teen pregnancy and illness among children.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I know it’s tough.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The reason Magic Johnson resigned from the AIDS Commission is because the statement you heard tonight from Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Bush is the longest and best statement he’s made about it in public.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I am proud of what we did at the Democratic Convention, putting 2 HIV-positive people on the platform, and I am proud of the leadership that I’m going to bring to this country in dealing with the AIDS crisis.

speaker: LEHRER
text: New question for Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Perot.

speaker: LEHRER
text: You have 2 minutes to answer, and Ann will ask it.

speaker: COMPTON
text: Mr.

speaker: COMPTON
text: Perot, even if you’ve got what people say are the guts to take on changes in the most popular, the most sacred of the entitlements, Medicare, people say you haven’t a prayer of actually getting anything passed in Washington.

speaker: COMPTON
text: Since a president isn’t a lone ranger, how in the world can you make some of those unpopular changes?

speaker: PEROT
text: Two ways.

speaker: PEROT
text: Number one, if I get there, it will be a very unusual and historical event — –because the people, not the special interests, put me there.

speaker: PEROT
text: I will have a unique mandate.

speaker: PEROT
text: I have said again and again, and this really upsets the establishment in Washington, that we’re going to inform the people in detail on the issues through an electronic town hall so that they really know what’s going on.

speaker: PEROT
text: They will want to do what’s good for our country.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, all these fellows with thousand-dollar suits and alligator shoes running up and down the halls of Congress that make policy now — the lobbyists, the PAC guys, the foreign lobbyists, and what-have-you, they’ll be over there in the Smithsonian, you know — — because we’re going to get rid of them, and the Congress will be listening to the people.

speaker: PEROT
text: And the American people are willing to have fair, shared sacrifice.

speaker: PEROT
text: They’re not as stupid as Washington thinks they are.

speaker: PEROT
text: The American people are bright, intelligent, caring, loving people who want a great country for their children and grandchildren.

speaker: PEROT
text: And they will make those sacrifices.

speaker: PEROT
text: So I welcome that challenge, and just watch — — because if the American people send me there, we’ll get it done.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now, everybody will faint in Washington.

speaker: PEROT
text: They’ve never seen anything happen in that town.

speaker: PEROT
text: This is a town where the White House says, Congress did it; Congress says, the White House did it.

speaker: PEROT
text: And I’m sitting there and saying, well, who else could be around, you know?

speaker: PEROT
text: Then when they get off by themselves, they say nobody did it.

speaker: PEROT
text: And yet the cash register’s empty and it used to have our money, the taxpayers’ money, in it, and we didn’t get the results.

speaker: PEROT
text: No, we’ll get it done.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Governor, one minute.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Ross, that’s a great speech, but it’s not quite that simple.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I mean, look at the facts.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Both parties in Washington, the president and the Congress, have cut Medicare.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The average senior citizen is spending a higher percentage of income on health care today than they were in 1965, before Medicare came in.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The president’s got another proposal to require them to pay $400 a year more for the next 5 years.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But if you don’t have the guts to control costs by changing the insurance system and taking on the bureaucracies and the regulation of health care in the private and public sector, you can’t fix this problem.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Costs will continue to spiral.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And just remember this, folks.

speaker: CLINTON
text: A lot of folks on Medicare are out there every day making the choice between food and medicine; not poor enough for Medicare-Medicaid, not wealthy enough to buy their medicine.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve met them, people like Mary Annie and Edward Davis in Nashua, New Hampshire.

speaker: CLINTON
text: All over this country, they cannot even buy medicine.

speaker: CLINTON
text: So let’s be careful.

speaker: CLINTON
text: When we talk about cutting health care costs, let’s start with the insurance companies and the people that are making a killing instead of making our people healthy.

speaker: LEHRER
text: One minute, President Bush.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, first place, I’d like to clear up something because every 4 years, the Democrats go around and say, Republicans are going to cut Social Security and Medicare.

speaker: BUSH
text: They started it again.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m the president that stood up and said, don’t mess with Social Security, and I’m not going to and we haven’t and we are not going to go after the Social Security recipient.

speaker: BUSH
text: I have one difference with Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: Perot on that because I don’t think we need to touch Social Security.

speaker: BUSH
text: What we do need to do, though, is control the growth of these mandatory programs.

speaker: BUSH
text: And Ross properly says, okay, there’s some pain in that.

speaker: BUSH
text: But Governor Clinton refuses to touch that, simply refuses.

speaker: BUSH
text: So what we’ve got to do is control it, let it grow for inflation, let it grow for the amount of new people added, population, and then hold the line.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I believe that is the way you get the deficit down, not by the tax-and-spend program that we hear every 4 years, whether it’s Mondale, Dukakis, whoever else it is.

speaker: BUSH
text: I just don’t believe we ought to do that.

speaker: BUSH
text: So hold the line on Social Security and put a cap on the growth of the mandatory program.

speaker: LEHRER
text: New question, it is for Governor Clinton, 2 -minute answer.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Sandy will ask it.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: Governor Clinton, Ann Compton has brought up Medicare.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: I remember in 1965, when Wilbur Mills of Arkansas, the chairman of Ways and Means, was pushing it through the Congress.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: The charge against it was it’s socialized medicine.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Bush made that charge.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: Well, he served with him 2 years later, in 1967, where I first met him.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: The 2nd point, though, is that it is now skyrocketing out of control.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: People want it.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: We say it’s going bonkers.

speaker: VANOCUR
text: Is not the Oregon plan applied to Medicaid rationing the proper way to go even though the federal government last August ruled that it violated the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990?

speaker: CLINTON
text: I thought the Oregon plan should at least have been allowed to be tried because at least the people in Oregon were trying to do something.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Let me go back to the main point, Sandy.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Bush is trying to run against Lyndon Johnson and Jimmy Carter and everybody in the world but me in this race.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I have proposed a managed competition plan for health care.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I will say again: you cannot control health care costs simply by cutting Medicare.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Look what’s happened.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The federal government has cut Medicare and Medicaid in the last few years, states have cut Medicaid — we’ve done it in Arkansas under budget pressures.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But what happens?

speaker: CLINTON
text: More and more people get on the rolls as poverty increases.

speaker: CLINTON
text: If you don’t control the health care costs of the entire system, you cannot get control of it.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Look at our program.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We set up a national ceiling on health care costs tied to inflation and population growth set by health care providers, not by the government.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We provide for managed competition, not government models, in every states.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And we control private and public health care costs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Now, just a few days ago a bipartisan commission of Republicans and Democrats — more Republicans than Democrats — said my plan will save the average family $1200 a year more than the Bush plan will by the year 2000, $2.

speaker: CLINTON
text: 2 trillion in the next 12 years, $400 billion a year by the end of this decade.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’ve got a plan to control health care costs.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But you can’t just do it by cutting Medicare; you have to take on the insurance companies, the bureaucracies.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And you have to have cost controls, yes.

speaker: CLINTON
text: But keep in mind we are spending 30% more on health care than any country in the world, any country, and yet we have 35 million people uninsured, we have no preventing and primary care.

speaker: CLINTON
text: The Oregon plan is a good start if the federal government is going to continue to abandon its responsibilities.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I say if Germany can cover everybody and keep costs under inflation, if Hawaii can cover 98% of their people at lower health care costs than the rest of us, if Rochester, New York, can do it with two-thirds of the cost of the rest of it, America can do it, too.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’m tired of being told we can’t.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I say we can.

speaker: CLINTON
text: We can do better, and we must.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President Bush, one minute.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, I don’t have time in 30 seconds, or whatever — a minute — to talk about our health care reform plan.

speaker: BUSH
text: The Oregon plan made some good sense, but it’s easy to dismiss the concerns of the disabled.

speaker: BUSH
text: As president I have to be sure that those waivers, which we’re approving all over the place, are covered under the law.

speaker: BUSH
text: Maybe we can work it out.

speaker: BUSH
text: But the Americans with Disabilities Act, speaking about sound and sensible civil rights legislation, was the most foremost piece of legislation passed in modern times, and so we do have something more than a technical problem.

speaker: BUSH
text: Governor Clinton clicked off the things — he’s going to take on insurance companies and bureaucracies.

speaker: BUSH
text: He failed to take on somebody else — the malpractice suit people, those that bring these lawsuits against — these frivolous trial lawyers’ lawsuits that are running the costs of medical care up 25 to 50 billion.

speaker: BUSH
text: And he refuses to put anything, controls, on these crazy lawsuits.

speaker: BUSH
text: If you want to help somebody, don’t run the costs up by making doctors have to have 5 or 6 tests where one would do for fear of being sued, or have somebody along the highway not stop to pick up a guy and help him because he’s afraid a trial lawyer will come along and sue him.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re suing each other too much and caring for each other too little.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Perot, one minute.

speaker: PEROT
text: We got the most expensive health care system in the world; it ranks behind 15 other nations when we come to life expectancy, and 22 other nations when we come to infant mortality.

speaker: PEROT
text: So we don’t have the best.

speaker: PEROT
text: Pretty simple, folks — if you’re paying more and you don’t have the best, if all else fails go copy the people who have the best who spend less, right?

speaker: PEROT
text: Well, we can do better than that.

speaker: PEROT
text: Again, we’ve got plans lying all over the place in Washington.

speaker: PEROT
text: Nobody ever implements them.

speaker: PEROT
text: Now I’m back to square one.

speaker: PEROT
text: If you want to stop talking about it and do it, then I’ll be glad to go up there and we’ll get it done.

speaker: PEROT
text: But if you just want to keep the music going, just stay traditional this next time around, and 4 years from now you’ll have everybody blaming everybody else for a bad health care system.

speaker: PEROT
text: Talk is cheap; words are plentiful, deeds are precious.

speaker: PEROT
text: Let’s get on with it.

speaker: LEHRER
text: And that’s exactly what we’re going to do.

speaker: LEHRER
text: That was, in fact, the final question and answer.

speaker: LEHRER
text: We’re now going to move to closing statements.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Each candidate will have up to 2 minutes.

speaker: LEHRER
text: The order, remember, was determined by drawing, and Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Perot, you are first.

speaker: PEROT
text: Well, it’s been a privilege to be able to talk to the American people tonight.

speaker: PEROT
text: I make no bones about it.

speaker: PEROT
text: I love this country.

speaker: PEROT
text: I love the principle it’s founded on.

speaker: PEROT
text: I love the people here.

speaker: PEROT
text: I don’t like to see the country’s principles violated.

speaker: PEROT
text: I don’t like to see the people in a deteriorating economy in a deteriorating country because our government has lost touch with the people.

speaker: PEROT
text: The people in Washington are good people.

speaker: PEROT
text: We just have a bad system.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’ve got to change the system.

speaker: PEROT
text: It’s time to do it because we have run up so much debt that time is no longer our friend.

speaker: PEROT
text: We’ve got to put our house in order.

speaker: PEROT
text: When you go to bed tonight, look at your children.

speaker: PEROT
text: Think of their dreams.

speaker: PEROT
text: Think of your dreams as a child and ask yourself, isn’t it time to stop talking about it?

speaker: PEROT
text: Isn’t it time to stop creating images?

speaker: PEROT
text: Isn’t it time to do it?

speaker: PEROT
text: Aren’t you sick of being treated like an unprogrammed robot?

speaker: PEROT
text: Every 4 years, they send you all kinds of messages to tell you how to vote and then go back to business as usual.

speaker: PEROT
text: They told you at the tax and budget summit that if you agreed to a tax increase, we could balance the budget.

speaker: PEROT
text: They didn’t tell you that that same year they increased spending $1.

speaker: PEROT
text: 83 for every dollar we increased taxes.

speaker: PEROT
text: That’s Washington in a nutshell right there.

speaker: PEROT
text: In the final analysis, I’m doing this for your children when you look at them tonight.

speaker: PEROT
text: There’s another group that I feel very close to, and these at the men and women who fought on the battlefield, the children — the families — of the ones who died and the people who left parts of their bodies over there.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’d never ask you to do anything for me, but I owe you this, and I’m doing it for you.

speaker: PEROT
text: And I can’t tell you what it means to me at these rallies when I see you and you come up and the look in your eyes — and I know how you feel and you know how I feel.

speaker: PEROT
text: And then I think of the older people who are retired.

speaker: PEROT
text: They grew up in the Depression.

speaker: PEROT
text: They fought and won World War II.

speaker: PEROT
text: We owe you a debt we can never repay you.

speaker: PEROT
text: And the greatest repayment I can ever give is to recreate the American dream for your children and grandchildren.

speaker: PEROT
text: I’ll give you everything I have, if you want me to do it.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Governor Clinton, your closing statement.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’d like to thank the people of St.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Louis and Washington University, the Presidential Debate Commission and all those who made this night possible.

speaker: CLINTON
text: And I’d like to thank those of you who are watching.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Most of all, I’d like to thank all of you who have touched me in some way over this last year, all the thousands of you whom I’ve seen.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’d like to thank the computer executives and the electronics executives in Silicon Valley, two-thirds of whom are Republicans who said they wanted to sign on to a change in America.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’d like to thank the hundreds of executives who came to Chicago, a third of them Republicans, who said they wanted to change.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’d like to thank the people who’ve started with Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Perot who’ve come on to help our campaign.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I’d like to thank all the folks around America that no one ever knows about — the woman that was holding the AIDS baby she adopted in Cedar Rapids, Iowa who asked me to do something more for adoption; the woman who stopped along the road in Wisconsin and wept because her husband had lost his job after 27 years; all the people who are having a tough time and the people who are winning but who know how desperately we need to change.

speaker: CLINTON
text: This debate tonight has made crystal clear a challenge that is as old as America — the choice between hope and fear, change or more of the same, the courage to move into a new tomorrow or to listen to the crowd who says things could be worse.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Mr.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Bush has said some very compelling things tonight that don’t quite square with the record.

speaker: CLINTON
text: He was president for 3 years before he proposed a health care plan that still hasn’t been sent to Congress in total; three years before an economic plan, and he still didn’t say tonight that that tax bill he vetoed raised taxes only on the rich and gave the rest of you a break — but he vetoed it anyway.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I offer a new direction.

speaker: CLINTON
text: Invest in American jobs, American education, control health care costs, bring this country together again.

speaker: CLINTON
text: I want the future of this country to be as bright and brilliant as its past, and it can be if we have the courage to change.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President Bush, your opposing statement.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me tell you a little what it’s like to be president.

speaker: BUSH
text: In the Oval Office, you can’t predict what kind of crisis is going to come up.

speaker: BUSH
text: You have to make tough calls.

speaker: BUSH
text: You can’t be on one hand this way and one hand another.

speaker: BUSH
text: You can’t take different positions on these difficult issues.

speaker: BUSH
text: And then you need a philosophical — I’d call it a philosophical underpinning.

speaker: BUSH
text: Mine for foreign affairs is democracy and freedom, and look at the dramatic changes around the world.

speaker: BUSH
text: The Cold War is over.

speaker: BUSH
text: The Soviet Union is no more and we’re working with a democratic country.

speaker: BUSH
text: Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, the Baltics are free.

speaker: BUSH
text: Take a look at the Middle East.

speaker: BUSH
text: We had to stand up against a tyrant.

speaker: BUSH
text: The US came together as we haven’t in many, many years.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we kicked this man out of Kuwait.

speaker: BUSH
text: And in the process, as a result of that will and that decision and that toughness, we now have ancient enemies talking peace in the Middle East.

speaker: BUSH
text: Nobody would have dreamed it possible.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I think the biggest dividend of making these tough calls is the fact that we are less afraid of nuclear war.

speaker: BUSH
text: Every parent out there has much less worry that their kids are going to be faced with nuclear holocaust.

speaker: BUSH
text: All this is good.

speaker: BUSH
text: On the domestic side, what we must do is have change that empowers people — not change for the sake of change, tax and spend.

speaker: BUSH
text: We don’t need to do that any more.

speaker: BUSH
text: What we need to do is empower people.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to invest and save.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to do better in education.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to do better in job retraining.

speaker: BUSH
text: We need to expand our exports, and they’re going very, very well, indeed.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we need to strengthen the American family.

speaker: BUSH
text: I hope as president that I’ve earned your trust.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve admitted it when I make a mistake, but then I go on and help, try to solve the problems.

speaker: BUSH
text: I hope I’ve earned your trust because a lot of being president is about trust and character.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I ask for your support for 4 more years to finish this job.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thank you very, very much.

text: Don’t go away yet.

speaker: LEHRER
text: I just want to thank the three panelists and thank the three candidates for participating — President Bush, Governor Clinton and Mr.

speaker: LEHRER

speaker: LEHRER
text: They will appear again together on October the 15th and again on October 19th, and next Tuesday there will be a debate among the three candidates for vice president.

speaker: LEHRER
